title: Improving the high stress abrasive wear resistance of medium carbon quenched and partitioned bainitic steel by controlling the phase transformation sequence
abstract: To address the high stress abrasive wear challenges in mining and metallurgical applications, the three microstructures of martensite-bainite-retained austenite, bainite-martensite-retained austenite and fully martensite were obtained by controlling the phase transformation sequence during heat treatment of the 0.3C steel. The effects of bainite and martensite phase transformation sequences on the microstructure evolution and the wear behavior of the steel were investigated. The results revealed that the transformation sequence of bainite followed by martensite (B-Q&P process) is more favorable for obtaining a finer multiphase microstructure comprising bainite-martensite-retained austenite than the reverse sequence of martensite followed by bainite transformation. This finer multiphase microstructure demonstrates not only a superior combination of strength (1584 MPa), toughness (135 J/cm2), hardness (48.4 HRC) and elongation (20.7 %), but also outstanding wear resistance. The wear loss of the B-Q&P sample is lower than that of the Q-B&P and Q&T samples, which can be ascribed to the improved toughness and enhanced surface microhardness that come from the transformation of retained austenite, the production of nanoscale crystalline structures, and the accumulation of dislocation defects. Some spalling damage characteristics can be observed on the wear surfaces of the Q-B&P and Q&T samples, whereas only delamination damage characteristics are present on the wear surface of the B-Q&P sample. The synergistic effect of a thicker deformation layer and 4.2 % retained austenite in the deformed microstructure of the B-Q&P sample suppresses downward crack propagation, thereby inhibiting spalling damage and enhancing wear resistance.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: High stress abrasive wear is a common phenomenon in mining applications, which results in significant economic loss by shortening the lifespan of mechanical parts [ 1 ]. Generally, steel subjected to high stress abrasives needs to endure heavy static and dynamic loads for prolonged durations. To improve the wear resistance of the steel, some strategies such as microalloying [ 2–4 ], surface treatments [ 5 , 6 ] and tailored microstructure by heat treatments [ 7–9 ] have been proposed, the last of which is considered to be one of the most direct and effective way.

Since a long time, the steel used for wear-resistant parts is usually treated by quenching and tempering (Q&T) process to obtain martensitic structure with higher strength and hardness [ 10 , 11 ]. The Q&T process has been considered to be the most economical and efficient treatment method for martensitic steels. However, the martensitic steel obtained from the Q&T process has limited resistance to wear due to their lower ductility [ 12 ]. In recent years, Speer introduced a process known as quenching and partitioning (Q&P) for achieving a mixed microstructure of martensite and retained austenite (RA) [ 13 ]. Wei pointed out that the superior wear resistance of Q&P steel relative to Q&T counterparts is attributed to its elevated RA content and refined martensite [ 14 ]. Yan and Lu reported that the Q&P steel possesses a higher strain hardening ability, which is controlled by the RA, leading to an obviously improved wear performance than that of Q&T steel [ 15 , 16 ]. Previous studies have conclusively demonstrated that wear resistance of steel is influenced not only by its initial hardness but also by other mechanical properties, such as ductility and toughness, caused by microstructural features, which significantly also affect the wear behavior of steel [ 1 , 9 , 17 , 18 ]. Although the Q&P process enhances the plasticity, but it has a limited effect on improving the toughness. This is primarily associated with the presence of blocky RA in addition to the film-like RA in the microstructure. Liu found that the presence of blocky RA will lead to a lower wear resistance due to the diminished toughness resulting from the formation of irregular fresh martensite during wear [ 19 ].

To reduce or eliminate the blocky RA, a modified Q&P process involving bainite transformation was designed to obtain a multiphase microstructure of martensite, bainite and retained austenite, which displays better mechanical properties [ 20–22 ]. Li compared the wear behavior of multiphase microstructure and martensite microstructure as well as bainite microstructure and found that the multiphase microstructure has superior wear resistance than the others [ 23 ].

In general, the bainite/martensite/retained austenite multiphase microstructure can be tailored by different phase transformation sequence routes during the modified Q&P process. Chen and Li reported that a finer multiphase microstructure can be produced by martensite transformation at the first quenching step and bainite transformation in the following step of partitioning [ 21 , 24 , 25 ]. The martensite formed can divide the prior austenite to refine the size of bainite formed during the partitioning step [ 26 , 27 ]. Huang and Li pointed out that bainite formed prior to the quenching step can also partition the prior austenite grains and refine the subsequent martensite microstructure [ 20 , 28 ]. In addition to the significant effect of different phase transformation sequence routes on the size of the multiphase microstructure, it also affects the stability and amount of RA. The stability and amount of RA is controlled by a competitive process of bainite formation and carbon partitioning from martensite to untransformed austenite [ 21 , 29–31 ]. However, until now, which phase transformation sequence routes can produce finer multiphase microstructure and obtain more stable retained austenite for the same steel as well as exhibit a better wear resistance has not been systematically investigated.

This study utilized two distinct heat treatment processes on medium carbon steel: 1) a quenching and bainite transformation plus partitioning process (hereafter called Q-B&P) to develop a martensite-bainite-retained austenite multiphase microstructure, and 2) a bainite transformation plus quenching and partitioning process (hereafter called B-Q&P) to create a bainite-martensite-retained austenite multiphase microstructure. The present work is an attempt to clarify the underlying effect mechanism of different phase transformation sequence routes on multiphase microstructure and wear behavior. In particular, the microstructure evolution during wear process and its correlation with the observed wear performance are discussed in detail, and the corresponding wear mechanisms are also examined. In addition, the medium carbon steel with martensite microstructure obtained by Q&T process was selected for comparison.

sections.heading: Materials and experimental details
paragraphs:
The chemical composition of studied steel is 0.28C–1.5Si-1.8Mn-1.3Cr. The temperature of martensite start transformation has been measured to be 310 °C, as shown in  Fig. 1 
                      .

To explore the influence of different phase transformation sequence routes on multiphase microstructure, two different processing routes, namely Q-B&P and B-Q&P, have been developed, as seen from  Fig. 2 
                      a and b. The studied steel subjected to the Q-B&P process was austenitized at 1000 °C for 10 min, and then quenched to 260 °C for 2 min with the martensite transformation, followed by the partitioned at 330 °C for 40 min with the purpose of the carbon partitioning and bainite transformation. The B-Q&P process also beginning with an austenization step at 1000 °C for 10 min and then salt quenching to 330 °C for 10 min to achieve partial bainite microstructure, followed by quenching to 200 °C for 30 min to undergo martensite transformation and promote carbon partitioning. The Q&T process involves a complete austenization at 1000 °C for 10 min and then quenched with oil to obtain martensite microstructure, as indicated in  Fig. 2 c. All samples treated by different processes were tempered at 280 °C for 120 min to release residual stress.

In the mineral transportation, the ore particles will have a relative rolling and sliding on the surface of component, resulting in cutting, fatigue spalling and other damage, and eventually cause wear failure of the component. In the current work, an MLD-10 model wear testing machine was applied to simulate the working condition of steel used for mineral transportation. The wear test schematic image and the morphology of abrasive particle are displayed in  Fig. 3 
                      . The sample is fixed on a fixture and surrounded by the solid abrasive. During wear testing, the fixture will rotate along with the sample, causing it to interact with the surrounding solid abrasive and undergo wear. For wear evaluation, samples with cubic dimensions of 5 × 15 × 35 mm 3  were prepared and the testing apparatus was operated at a rotational velocity of 200 revolutions per minute (RPM). The quartz sand particles with a hardness value range of 1000∼1200 HV are used as abrasive and its average size is about 3 mm, as shown in  Fig. 3 b. Each cycle lasted 20 min, after which the quartz sand particles were refreshed. This process was repeated 6 times under the same conditions. Following the wear test, the weight loss was measured by an electronic scale.

The toughness value of steel treated by different processes was conducted on JB-300B impact machine with the size of 10 mm × 10 mm × 55 mm. Strength and elongation were measured by DDL100 tensile machine with the size of 85 mm × 6 mm × 4 mm. The macrohardness and microhardness was conducted on a HR-150 Rockwell hardness tester with a 150 kg load and a DHV-1000Z Vickers hardness tester with a 200 g load, respectively. Five discrete hardness measurements were statistically processed to determine the mean hardness value. The microstructure evolutions were analyzed by means of SEM (S–3400 N) and TEM (G2 F20 S). The surface morphologies after wear testing were analyzed via a OLS5100 laser scanning confocal microscope. The sample was characterized using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) system on a SEM. EBSD data were collected at an acceleration voltage of 20 kV with a step size of 150 nm, and subsequently analyzed using EDAX-TSL postprocessing software.

The retained austenite was tested by a DX-2700 X-ray diffractometer, and the amount was determined by employing the (211)α and (220)γ [ 32 ]. For the B-Q&P process, to distinguish between bainite and martensite, the samples were held isothermal at 330 °C for 10 min and then quenched in water to room temperature without tempering. The volume fraction of bainite was quantitatively determined using optical microscope (OM; CMM-20) equipped with an image analysis system according to Chinese standard GB/T 18876.1-2002 [ 33 ]. For the Q-B&P process, the volume fraction of martensite can be calculated by Koistinen-Marburger relationship [ 34 ].

sections.heading: Microstructure analysis and mechanical properties
paragraphs:
The SEM characterization in  Fig. 4 
                          demonstrates the microstructure of samples following distinct processing stages. As shown in 4a and 4b, both B-Q&P and Q-B&P processed steels display microstructures containing bainitic ferrite sheaves and martensite sheaves. In contrast, microstructural characterization of the Q&T sample revealed a fully martensitic constitution and exhibited a typical sheaf morphology, as shown in  Fig. 4 c.

Fig. 5 
                          presents combined image quality (IQ) and inverse pole figure (IPF) maps, and boundary misorientation distribution maps. It is widely recognized that bainite and martensite share similar complex substructures that can be broadly categorized into ascending levels of laths, blocks, and packets, which exist within prior austenite grains. As depicted in  Fig. 5ã ,c, the size of blocks and packets in the B-Q&P sample is smaller than those in the Q-B&P and Q&T samples. Additionally, it can also be observed from Fig. 5d, e, and 5f Fig. 5 d, e, and 5f that the proportion of high-angle boundaries (above 15°) in the B-Q&P sample (66.5 %) is higher than in both the Q-B&P (61.3 %) and Q&T samples (55.4 %). The high-angle boundaries in bainite and martensite microstructures predominantly include boundaries of prior austenite grains, packets, and blocks. The proportion of prior austenite grains boundaries in these high-angle boundaries remains consistent across all samples due to the identical austenitization step performed at 1000 °C for 10 min. Therefore, the increased high-angle boundaries in the B-Q&P sample can be attributed to the increased boundaries of packets and blocks, resulting from their refinement.

To gain a clearer understanding of the microstructure of the steel subjected to different treatments, TEM characterization was performed on the samples. Both the B-Q&P and Q-B&P samples exhibited a microstructure composed of lath martensite, lath bainite and retained austenite ( Fig. 6 
                         a and b). In contrast, the Q&T sample was characterized by lath martensite and retained austenite in its microstructure ( Fig. 6 c). The retained austenite in the B-Q&P and Q&T samples displays a filmy morphology, whereas in the Q-B&P sample, it appears in both thin film and blocky morphologies. It should be noted that martensite laths in the B-Q&P sample are finer in dimension than those observed in both Q-B&P and Q&T samples. The B-Q&P sample's bainitic ferrite, developed through 330 °C isothermal transformation, exhibited unrestricted growth of single plate sheave morphologies governed by crystallographic orientation until adjacent sheaves encountered one another, leading to growth cessation. Bainite sheaves formed during isothermal holding partition prior austenite grains into confined domains. Subsequent martensite nucleation and evolution within these untransformed austenite zones result in a fined martensite lath size.

The Q-B&P sample operates under an analogous mechanism: martensitic sheaves generated during the quenching phase subdivide prior austenite grains, simultaneously refining bainitic structures evolving in the partitioning stage. However,  Fig. 6 b reveals that the dimensions of bainite laths in the Q-B&P sample are larger relative to those in the B-Q&P sample. This difference can be attributed to the extended partitioning duration of 40 min, which promotes the merging of bainite laths (such as B1 and B2 in  Fig. 6 b), leading to the coalesced bainite [ 35 ].

Based on the discussion above, it can be concluded that the phase transformation sequence of first bainite followed by martensite is more favorable for obtaining a finer multiphase structure than the sequence of first martensite followed by bainite.

Fig. 7 
                          shows representative tensile engineering stress-strain curves for samples treated by different processes, with corresponding mechanical properties listed in  Table 1 
                         . All curves exhibit elastic deformation, a plastic deformation plateau, and final fracture. The B-Q&P treated sample displays a broader strain hardening plateau before necking compared with the Q-B&P and Q&T treated samples, indicating that the B-Q&P sample has better plastic deformation capacity. As indicted in  Table 1  and  Fig. 7 , the Q&T sample demonstrates a tensile strength of 1671 MPa and a hardness of 50.3 HRC, exceeding the values recorded for both Q-B&P and B-Q&P samples. This higher strength and hardness of the Q&T sample mainly result from its fully martensite microstructure combined with a higher dislocation density. However, the Q-B&P sample registers significantly lower strength (1498 MPa) and hardness (46.5 HRC) compared to the Q&T sample. As demonstrated in  Fig. 5 b, the lath-like microstructure in the Q-B&P sample exhibits a coarser appearance as compared with the Q&T sample. Additionally, martensite formed during quenching will undergo tempering in the subsequent isothermal partitioning at 330 °C for 40 min. These factors primarily account for the reduced strength and hardness noted in the Q-B&P sample. In comparison to the Q-B&P and Q&T samples, the B-Q&P sample demonstrates superior comprehensive properties, having a strength of 1584 MPa and a hardness of 48.4 HRC. Moreover, the B-Q&P sample exhibits significantly enhanced elongation (20.7 %) and toughness (135 J/cm 2 ) compared to both the Q-B&P and Q&T samples, attributable to its finer lath-like microstructure and higher RA content (9.1 %).

Fig. 8 
                          displays typical fracture surfaces of impact samples treated by different processes. All samples show cleavage facets with dimples, indicating quasi-cleavage fracture. Notably, B-Q&P and Q-B&P samples exhibit more dimples than the Q&T sample, consistent with enhanced impact toughness. Moreover, the B-Q&P sample has greater dimple density and depth than the Q-B&P sample, indicating that the sample first yields and undergoes relatively sufficient deformation during the impact process, which consumes a large amount of energy. Therefore, the B-QP sample exhibits the highest impact toughness of 135 J/cm 2 .

sections.heading: Wear surface characterization
paragraphs:
Fig. 9 
                          presents the SEM and 3D laser scanning confocal images showing the wear surface morphologies of steel treated with different processes. The wear surfaces of all samples after 120 min of wear testing exhibit relatively rough surface morphologies resulting from repeated impact and rolling-sliding caused by abrasive particles. The surface roughness Sa for the B-Q&P, Q-B&P, and Q&T samples are 4.069 μm ( Figs. 9 c), 7.863 μm ( Figs. 9 f), and 11.048 μm ( Fig. 9 i), respectively. Previous work has reported that surface roughness can reflect wear behavior, with smaller surface roughness indicating better wear resistance [ 36 ]. Therefore, the B-Q&P sample, which has lower surface roughness, may have a better capacity to resist wear compared to the other two samples.

In the current study, the high-stress abrasive wear process consists of two main stages: an impact stage and a rolling-sliding stage, which interact to create the final wear surface characteristics. At the beginning of the wear testing, the surface will be subjected to plastic strain because of the repeated collision and rolling-sliding caused by abrasive particles. When the plastic strain reaches a critical limit, resulting in plastic exhaustion, surface cracks will be initiated. As the testing progresses, some of these cracks propagate shallowly along a horizontal direction parallel to the surface, resulting in the delamination. Some cracks can penetrate deep into the material, removing thicker wear products and ultimately causing spalling damage. As shown in  Fig. 9 , all samples exhibit delamination damage, with spalling characteristics observed exclusively on both the Q-B&P and Q&T samples. Moreover, the degree of spalling damage in the Q&T sample ( Fig. 9 g and h) is more severe compared to its Q-B&P counterpart ( Fig. 9 d and e), which can be attributed to its lower toughness and plastic deformation capacity. As seen from  Figs. 5 and 6 , and  Table 1 , B-Q&P sample exhibits a smaller microstructure, with more high-angle boundaries (66.5 %) and retained austenite (9.1 %). The finer microstructure and more retained austenite transformation during the wear process are conducive to the coordination of plastic deformation and the release of local stress, thereby delaying crack initiation and hindering crack propagation. Furthermore, the higher number of high-angle boundaries helps prevent cracks from propagating deep into the sample. Consequently, no obvious spalling damage is observed on the B-Q&P sample ( Fig. 9 a and b). Besides the delamination and spalling damage, the cutting and ploughing characteristics are universally manifested on all samples' worn surfaces. A comparative reduction in cutting/ploughing severity is observed on the Q&T sample's wear surface relative to B-Q&P and Q-B&P counterparts, which is related to its higher bulk hardness. In contrast, during the wear process, the rolling-sliding of abrasive particles can relatively easily remove the material on the surface of the B-Q&P and Q-B&P samples which have lower bulk hardness, leaving behind some groove caused by cutting and ploughing ( Fig. 9 a and d) and plastic deformation ridges ( Fig. 9 b and e). However, the groove depth of the B-Q&P sample is shallower compared to the Q-B&P sample, attributable to its higher bulk hardness and surface hardening effect resulting from the persistent transformation of filmy RA.

sections.heading: Microhardness after wear testing
paragraphs:
The measured microhardness of all samples after 120 min high stress abrasive wear are summarized in  Table 2 
                         .  Fig. 10 
                          illustrates the microhardness measurement profiles along the depth from the worn surface. All samples exhibit a gradual decline in microhardness with greater subsurface depth, ultimately converging toward the bulk material's baseline microhardness. Specifically, the near-surface microhardness values show significant enhancements: Q-B&P sample increases from 509 HV 0.2  to 587 HV 0.2 , B-Q&P sample from 526 HV 0.2  to 623 HV 0.2 , and Q&T sample demonstrates the most substantial improvement from 542 HV 0.2  to 651 HV 0.2 . Corresponding to these measurements, the microhardness enhancement percentages amount to 15.3 % for Q-B&P, 18.4 % for B-Q&P, and notably 20.1 % for Q&T samples.

To establish the correlation between microstructural evolution and microhardness characteristics, samples after 120 min high stress abrasive wear test were systematically analyzed through combined XRD and TEM characterization.  Fig. 11 
                         c shows the depth dependent XRD patterns of Q&T sample, revealing exclusive presence of ferrite (α-phase) with retained austenite (γ-phase) content below the detection limit due to its minimal concentration. As demonstrated in  Fig. 11 a and b, B-Q&P and Q-B&P samples initially contained approximately 9.1 % and 5.8 % retained austenite in their matrices, respectively, but exhibited complete depletion of γ-phase at 20 μm depth below wear surface, indicating complete stress triggered transformation of retained austenite into martensite through abrasive wear. Notably, at 40 μm depth, the B-Q&P sample maintained 4.2 % retained austenite, contrasting with the Q-B&P sample's exclusive α-phase composition. This contrast confirms superior stability of RA in the B-Q&P sample under mechanical stress induced phase transformation conditions [ 28 , 37 ].

Fig. 12 
                          presents TEM micrographs of subsurface regions at a depth of approximately 20 μm. The microstructure across all samples is characterized by nearly homogeneous near-equiaxed nanocrystalline grains, resulting from severe plastic deformation during high stress abrasive wear testing. The average nanocrystalline grain sizes measured at this depth are approximately 107 nm for B-Q&P, 126 nm for Q-B&P, and 94 nm for Q&T samples. Insets in  Fig. 12 a, c, and 12e display selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns with polycrystalline rings indexed to BCC structure of α-Fe. This evidence indicates that martensitic transformation of RA occurs at about 20 μm depth in both B-Q&P and Q-B&P samples, consistent with XRD observations. Moreover, comparative analysis reveals that B-Q&P and Q-B&P samples exhibit significantly high dislocations arising from martensitic transformation of RA and plastic deformation induced by high stress abrasive wear, compared to those in the Q&T sample.

Therefore, it can be inferred that the enhanced microhardness of the B-QP and Q-B&P samples primarily result from three interrelated mechanisms: the deformation-triggered martensitic transformation of RA, the development of nanoscale crystalline structures, and substantial accumulation of dislocation defects within the microstructure. Nevertheless, the most pronounced enhancement in microhardness observed in the Q&T sample predominantly stems from the production of smaller nanocrystalline and increased dislocation density.

Fig. 13 
                          presents TEM micrographs of subsurface microstructural features at approximately 40 μm depth in both B-Q&P and Q-B&P samples. Microstructural characterization reveals a structural transition to non-lath morphology in the B-Q&P sample, accompanied by some filmy retained austenite distributed within the matrix ( Fig. 13 a). This observation aligns with the XRD results shown in  Fig. 11 a. Compared with the B-Q&P sample, the Q-B&P sample demonstrates complete elimination of both filmy and blocky retained austenite following wear testing ( Fig. 13 b), suggesting distinct retained austenite stability behaviors between the two processed samples.

sections.heading: Wear loss after wear test
paragraphs:
Fig. 14 
                          illustrates the dependence of cumulative mass loss on time. The wear loss shows an increasing trend with extended wear time. The final cumulative wear mass loss reached 163 mg for B-Q&P, 182 mg for Q-B&P, and 219 mg for Q&T samples. The wear-induced mass variations were statistically evaluated through parametric ANOVA, with statistical significance predefined at  p  = 0.05 confidence level.  Table 3 
                          provides the statistical significance analyses for different samples based on the hypothesis that microstructure plays an important role in determining wear loss. Except for wear time of 80 min, the mass loss change was statistically significant ( p  < 0.05). At 80 min of wear time, the average mass loss of the Q&T, Q-B&P and B-Q&P samples was slightly different, though the statistical significance was much lower ( p  > 0.05). The above findings confirm that microstructure significantly influences wear loss behavior.

It is generally accepted that wear performance is predominantly governed by material hardness levels. When wear time is less than 80 min, Q&T processed steel with higher matrix hardness (542 HV 0.2 ) is more effective in resisting high stress abrasive wear, followed by B-Q&P and Q-B&P processed steel. When wear time is more than 80 min, the mass loss of Q&T processed steel exceeds the other two samples. Meanwhile, it's worthy of note that the B-Q&P processed steel with lower hardness has the lowest wear loss. Therefore, it is reasonable to believe that other factors besides hardness affect the wear performance.

As illustrated in  Fig. 9 , the B-Q&P sample with higher toughness of 135 J/cm 2  displays delamination on its wear surface, while some spalling features are visible on the surface of the Q-B&P and Q&T processed steels. In general, delamination and spalling are caused by local fracture of the material due to crack propagation. The mass loss resulting from spalling is significantly greater than that caused by delamination. The higher the toughness, the greater the energy consumed in the crack propagation process, the shallower the crack propagation depth, and the more likely material delamination occurs, thereby reducing wear loss. Thus, the enhanced wear resistance of the B-Q&P processed steel originates from the synergistic interplay between its higher toughness and enhanced surface hardness, which collectively minimize wear loss during high stress abrasive wear testing.

sections.heading: Subsurface characterization
paragraphs:
Fig. 15 
                          shows the subsurface images of samples following a 120 min high stress wear test. The subsurface region of B-Q&P processed steel exhibits a relatively minor crack situated at shallow depth beneath the wear surface, accompanied by shallow, gently sloping depressions resulting from material removal. These subsurface features demonstrate strong consistency with the delamination damage patterns observed on the wear surface of B-Q&P processed steel ( Fig. 9 a). However, in addition to obvious plastic deformation layer and delamination damage, the distinct spalling damage and voids are observed in the subsurface region of the Q-B&P sample. It should be noted that the wear surface of the Q&T sample exhibits a distinct white-etching layer, which can be confirmed by the TEM ( Fig. 12 e and f). Within the worn subsurface region, interfacial cracks are observed between the white etching layer and deformed matrix.

The data in  Table 1  demonstrate that the B-Q&P processed steel with finer multiphase microstructure exhibits superior elongation (20.7 %) to the Q-B&P sample, correlating directly with enhanced ductility. This promotes greater deformation compatibility during wear, resulting in a thicker plastically deformed layer for the B-Q&P sample compared to the Q-B&P sample ( Fig. 15 a). The formation of a thicker plastically deformed layer necessitates greater energy expenditure during wear testing, thereby reducing the energy available for crack initiation and propagation. Additionally, the presence of 4.2 % retained austenite within the plastically deformed layer (as identified in  Figs. 11a and 13 a) serves to inhibit crack propagation through the strain-induced martensitic transformation (TRIP) mechanism. The synergistic interaction of these two properties leads to the cracks being restricted by the deformed layer, which hinders the downward crack propagation in depth, thus showing a delamination damage model.

In contrast, the Q-B&P processed steel exhibits significantly greater crack penetration depth relative to its B-Q&P counterpart due to a thinner plastically deformed layer and the absence of retained austenite within this deformation zone. These two factors prevent the Q-B&P samples from confining cracks within the plastic deformation layer like the B-Q&P samples do, resulting in some cracks extending deeper. Consequently, the subsurface of Q-B&P processed steel reveals a pronounced spalling induced material loss in conjunction with delamination damage, as shown in  Fig. 15 b. In addition, some voids are also detected within the subsurface region of the Q-B&P processed steel. As previously established, the blocky retained austenite is relatively unstable and will undergo strain-assisted martensitic transformation to form untempered fresh martensite even under low strain conditions. The distinct elastoplastic behavior of the newly formed martensite and parent matrix, originating from their divergent strength and ductility characteristics, will produce an inhomogeneous stress distribution in the process of wear testing [ 38 , 39 ]. Such heterogeneous stress distribution drives the formation of voids at martensite/matrix interfaces, ultimately accelerating material removal through enhanced microcrack coalescence pathways, which will contribute to the wear process [ 40 ].

Generally, the spalling damage caused by a larger crack propagation length and depth leads to increased wear loss compared to delamination damage. Thus, the Q-B&P sample exhibits a higher wear loss than the B-Q&P sample.

As displayed in  Fig. 15 c, the Q&T processed steel shows obvious white-etching layer on the wear surface. It has been reported that the white-etching layer can exhibit an extremely high hardness level, which is consistent with the hardness test results in section  3.3 , where the Q&T processed steel has the highest surface hardness (651HV 0.2 ) after the wear test [ 41 ]. In addition, some interfacial cracks can be observed at the boundary between the white-etching layer and the matrix due to the poor deformation compatibility between them. In the process of the high stress wear, a portion of the interfacial cracks exhibits propagation along a direction parallel to the wear surface, leading to the removal of white-etching layer from the sample, which contributes to the delamination damage. The remaining interfacial cracks propagate downward into the sample depth, finally leading to the spalling damage. Previous works indicated that besides hardness, the plasticity and toughness of the sample are also crucial factors influencing wear performance [ 23 , 42 ].Compared to the B-Q&P and Q-B&P samples, the lower elongation (15.6 %) and impact toughness (101 J/cm 2 ) of the Q&T sample limits energy absorption, resulting in increased energy availability for crack propagation into the material depth, which will help for the more severe spalling damage. Thus, the Q&T sample with highest surface hardness exhibits the highest wear weight loss.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
The key conclusions of this study are summarized below. 
                         
                            (1) 
                            In contrast to Q&T and Q-B&P processed steels, the B-Q&P processed steel featuring refined multiphase microstructure (bainite/martensite/retained austenite) demonstrates synergistic enhancement in mechanical properties (ultimate strength: 1584 MPa, impact toughness: 135 J/cm 2 , Rockwell hardness: 48.4 HRC, ductility: 20.7 % elongation), coupled with exceptional wear performance under high stress abrasive conditions. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            The wear surfaces of all samples show delamination damage, whereas that for the Q&T and Q-B&P processed steels display spalling damage. Comparative analysis indicates the Q-B&P processed steel demonstrates markedly reduced spallation severity relative to its Q&T counterpart. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            The deformation-triggered martensitic transformation of RA, the nanoscale crystalline structures formation and the substantial accumulation of dislocation defects bring about a greater microhardness of the B-Q&P processed steel. However, the highest surface microhardness obtained from the Q&T processed steel is primarily ascribed to the white-etching layer formation. 
                         
                         
                            (4)
